content.content: LONG TIME DERIVATION OF THE BOLTZMANN EQUATION FROM HARD SPHERE DYNAMICS
YU DENG, ZAHER HANI, AND XIAO MA

Abstract. We provide a rigorous derivation of Boltzmann’s kinetic equation from the hard sphere system for rarefied gas, which is valid for arbitrarily long times, as long as the solution to the Boltzmann equation exists. This extends Lanford’s landmark theorem [40], which justifies this derivation for a suficiently short time. In a companion paper [24], we connect this derivation to existing literature on hydrodynamic limits. This completes the resolution of Hilbert’s Sixth Problem pertaining to the derivation of fluid equations from Newton’s laws, in the case of a rarefied, hard sphere gas.

The general strategy follows the paradigm introduced by the first two authors for the long-time derivation of the wave kinetic equation in wave turbulence theory. This is based on propagating a long-time cumulant ansatz, which keeps memory of the full collision history of the relevant particles, by an important partial time expansion. The heart of the matter is proving the smallness of these cumulants in

, which can be reduced to combinatorial properties for the associated diagrams which we call molecules. These properties are then proved by devising an elaborate cutting algorithm, which is a major novelty of this work.

YU DENG, ZAHER HANI, AND XIAO MA

Dating back to the year 1872, Boltzmann’s kinetic theory is one of the most profound and revolutionary scientific ideas ever introduced. At the heart of this theory lies Boltzmann’s kinetic equation which gives an efective macroscopic description of the statistics of a large system of microscopic interacting particles. A significant feature of this theory, which caused some controversy at the time of its inception, is the fact that the macroscopic description is given by a time-irreversible equation (i.e. with an entropy functional that increases forward in time), which is derived from a microscopic system satisfying the time-reversible Newton’s laws of motion. This is known as the emergence of the arrow of time.

Unsurprisingly, this profound physical theory prompted the deep mathematical question, namely to rigorously justify the derivation of Boltzmann’s equation starting from Newton’s laws. This question was asked by Hilbert, in his address at the International Congress of Mathematicians in 1900, as the sixth problem in his celebrated list of outstanding mathematical problems for the twentieth century. More precisely, he proposed the question of giving a mathematically rigorous derivation for the macroscopic equations of fluids, such as the Euler and Navier-Stokes equations, from the Newtonian laws governing microscopic particle interactions, with the derivation of Boltzmann’s kinetic equation as a crucial intermediate step. This prob lem requires justifying two limits: (i) the kinetic limit where we pass from the (microscopic) Newtonian dynamics for an N-particle system to Boltzmann’s kinetic equation for the one-particle density function in the limit
and (ii) the hydrodynamic limit where we pass from Boltzmann’s kinetic equation to the (macroscopic) equations of fluid motion in the limit where the collision rate goes to infinity.

Despite being the subject of extensive study in the last century, this problem remained open for more than 120 years after it was first announced. While the second hydrodynamic limit is much better understood (see the discussions in Section 1.4.1 below), the main dificulty in the resolution of Hilbert’s sixth problem lies in justifying the first kinetic limit, which is the subject of this manuscript. In this direction, the state of art can be briefly summarized as follows, see Section 1.2 for a more extensive review. A landmark result of Lanford [40] in 1975 provides the rigorous derivation of the Boltzmann equation for suficiently short time. This result has since been completed, improved, and further developed by diferent groups of authors (see for example Illner-Pulvirenti [34], Gallagher-Saint Raymond-Texier [27] and more recent works [49, 8, 9, 11, 7] concerning fluctuations). However, all these works are still restricted to perturbative regimes, either under short-time or near-vacuum conditions or at the exact Maxwellian equilibrium.

The main result of this paper fills this gap, and thus completes the justification of the first limit needed for the resolution of Hilbert’s sixth problem. More precisely, we provide a rigorous derivation of Boltzmann’s equation from hard sphere dynamics, for arbitrarily long time that covers the full lifespan of the Boltzmann solution. This solution may come from any given initial data, which can also be arbitrarily large. In particular, if a solution to the Boltzmann equation exists globally, then our derivation is valid for all finite times, and times going (slowly) to infinity. In the companion work [24], we will connect this to the second hydrodynamic limit, thus giving a full resolution to Hilbert’s sixth problem (see Section 1.4.1).

1.2. Background and history. We briefly discuss the background and history of the rigorous derivation of Boltzmann’s equation, and the closely related problem of deriving its wave counterpart, i.e. the wave kinetic equation in wave turbulence theory.

1.2.1. Particle systems and the Boltzmann equation. The study of large particle systems has a long history starting from the beginning of the theory of statistical physics. The kinetic theory, which lies at the heart of nonequilibrium statistical physics, started with the following genius observation of Boltzmann [12, 13]: assuming independence of states between diferent particles, the full statistics of the system can be described by a single closed efective equation, namely the kinetic equation, in the limit of infinite degrees of freedom.

The first instance of what is now known as the Boltzmann equation was written down in the 1870s; since then, the mathematical justification of this limiting process has been a major challenge. The main dificulty comes from justifying the assumption of (asymptotic) independence of diferent particles, which is known as the Stosszahlansatz or molecular chaos. The formulation of this problem as known today was first put forward by Grad, and the works of Cercignani and Grad in the 1950s introduced the important idea of the BBGKY hierarchy to this subject. In the mean time, a simplified model was also introduced and studied by Kac ([38], see also subsequent and related developments [47, 51, 43, 44, 45]). Motivated by these contributions, Lanford [40] (see also King [39]) was able to set a first milestone in this subject, by proving the molecular chaos assumption and deriving the Boltzmann equation for suficiently small time.

Since [40], there have been numerous results devoted to the derivation of the Boltzmann equation and related problems. We do not attempt to be exhaustive in recounting the vast literature, but only list some of the most important ones below; see the surveys [53, 6, 10] and references therein for the other contributions.
• Illner-Pulvirenti [34] (see also [35]), which obtained a long-time result but for the near-vacuum case (i.e. the collision rate
• Gallagher-Saint Raymond-Texier [27], which completed and refined the result of [40], and obtained explicit convergence rates;

• Pulvirenti-Simonella [49], which obtained explicit decay rates for cumulants associated with the hard sphere system, with the exponent proportional to the number of involved particles, again in the short-time regime;

• Bodineau-Gallagher-Saint Raymond [3, 4, 5], which studied the related problems of deriving Brownian motion, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, and the Stokes-Fourier system from the hard sphere dynamics, by passing through a linearized Boltzmann equation;

• Bodineau-Gallagher-Saint Raymond-Simonella [8, 9, 11, 7], which investigated the further question of deriving the equation for fluctuations, either for short time, or for longer times but at the exact Maxwellian equilibrium.

Finally, apart from the question of deriving the kinetic equations, there has also been a huge literature concerning the solution theory of these equations (Boltzmann, Landau etc.). In general strong solutions exist in local and perturbative settings, but only weak solutions are known globally (see however [30, 36] on recent global existence results in the homogeneous setting). We will not elaborate on this, but refer to the reviews in [56, 57] and references therein.

1.2.2. Wave turbulence and the wave kinetic equation. One of the most important developments in the physics of the twentieth century was the emergence of quantum physics as a theory to describe subatomic particle dynamics. A central idea here is the particle-wave duality, which contributed to an exponential rise in the physical and mathematical interest in nonlinear wave systems. This led to the recasting of many classical particle theories in the context of interacting wave systems, including the theory of nonequilibrium statistical physics for waves, known as the wave turbulence or wave kinetic theory.

Same as the particle case, the wave kinetic theory aims at describing the statistics of a wave system using a closed equation for the lowest order correlation; usually this is the second moment of the wave field, as opposed to the one-particle density function in the kinetic theory for particles. The role of the Boltzmann equation is then played by the wave kinetic equation (WKE). For instance, in dimension
when the wave system is modeled by the cubic nonlinear Schr¨odinger equation, the corresponding wave kinetic equation takes the form

term in (1.19) is absent), where we use the same notation as in (1.14). The wave kinetic equations, similar to (1.19) but for diferent wave systems, were first introduced in the work of Peierls [48] in 1929 for anharmonic crystals. This was shortly followed by works of Nordheim [37] and Uehling and Uhlenbeck [55] in the context of quantum gases. Since then, the theory has attracted a great deal of attention from mathematicians and physicists, and has developed into a rich and broad subject. In particular, these contributions included the influential works of Hasselmann [31, 32] in 1962–1963, which applied the wave kinetic theory to ocean waves and led to the modern methods of ocean surface forecasting, as well as the work of Zakharov [58] in 1965, which provided a systematic approach to the theory and how it can be used to understand turbulent phenomena for waves. In [58], Zakharov also introduced the notion of Kolmogorov-Zakharov spectra, along the same lines as Kolmogorov’s theory of hydrodynamic turbulence. It is for this reason that the theory is also commonly known as wave turbulence theory. We refer the reader to [46] for a textbook treatment.

Mathematically, the study of the derivation of wave kinetic equations like (1.19) started with the work of Spohn [54]. For linear models, this program was completed in Erd¨os-Yau [26] and Erd¨os-Salmhofer-Yau [25]. For the full nonlinear problem, an important early milestone was due to Lukkarinen-Spohn [41] and subsequent partial results were obtained in [14, 19, 16, 17]. We refer the reader to the introduction of [22] for a more exhaustive historical recount. The full derivation of (1.19) in the short-time regime was obtained by the first two authors [20, 21, 22], serving as the wave-counterpart of Lanford’s theorem.

Recently, in [23], the first two authors have extended the derivation of (1.19) to arbitrarily long times that cover the full lifespan of solutions to (1.19). We remark that the result of [23] is parallel to Theorem 1, not only conceptually but also on a very concrete level. In fact, while the proof in the current paper is self-contained, many of the key ideas in this proof are obtained by adapting the ideas from the proof in [23] to the particle setting. In Section 2.5 we will make a detailed comparison between the proofs in [23] and in the current paper, including both similarities and diferences.

1.3. Main ideas of the proof. In this subsection, we present a mostly philosophical description of the proof, its strategy, and its most important ideas. A more elaborate and concrete discussion of these ideas can be found in Section 2.
To a large extent, the framework of the proof in this paper is the same as that in [23]. Below we will explain this framework in the current context of particle systems.

2.5. Comparison between wave and particle systems. As mentioned in Section 1.2, the proof in this paper is deeply inspired by that in the wave setting by the first two authors [23]. Here we make a brief comparison between the two proofs, in terms of their similarities and diferences. In the case of wave kinetic theory, the microscopic system in [23] is given by the nonlinear Schr¨odinger (NLS) equation on a torus
of size L, with a nonlinearity of strength α. The lowest-order nontrivial statistical quantity is the second moment of the Fourier modes
is the Fourier transform of the solution
to the NLS equation, which is to be approximated by the solution of the (homogeneous) wave kinetic equation (1.19), in the limit
. This kinetic limit is taken under an appropriate choice of scaling law between L and
At a conceptual level, the two proofs are very similar. The fundamental dificulty represented by the divergence of the series expansion on the long time interval

is the same, and the same goes for the need to create an arrow of time where, in both cases, the microscopic system is time-reversible but the limiting kinetic equation is irreversible. The idea of performing a partial expansion, where one refrains from expanding the lowest order statistic (the
here, and the second moments in the wave case) but expands the cumulants all the way to time
, is also the same. This keeps track of all the relevant collisions or interactions on the long time interval
that afect the cumulants at time

Even at a more technical level, there are uncanny similarities between the two proofs. First, both proofs start with a truncation of the dynamics in order to control the size of the diagrams appearing in the cumulant expansions. Also, in both proofs, the needed cumulant estimate is reduced to a combinatorial problem that is resolved through an elaborate algorithm. This combinatorial problem, in both cases, involves th combinatorial structure of molecules, which are formed by atoms that represent collisions or interactions. While the algorithms are vastly diferent in the wave case and particle case, there is an important similarity in the gain mechanism. As shown in Section 2.3, the basic unit of gain here is the special structure of {33} molecules; similarly, in the wave case, the basic unit of gain also comes from the {33} molecules and the associated five-vector counting problem.

All this being said, the analogy between the particle and wave kinetic theories has its limitations, and despite the above similarities, each proof carries its own distinct set of challenges. In the wave case, a large box limit needs to be performed to go from the discrete Fourier space of

to the continuum setting of the wave kinetic equation (1.19). This links the wave kinetic theory to some deep number theory problems, which seems to be absent in the particle setting. Also, the Feynman diagram expansion for the NLS equation turns out to converge only conditionally and not absolutely, and requires highly nontrivial cancellations between arbitrarily large diagrams, which is another distinctive feature and novelty of [23]. On the other hand, the cumulant expansion in the particle setting is technically more involved, due to the application of inclusion exclusion principle and the resulting notion of overlaps, which does not seem to be have an analog in the wave case. Also the main algorithm in the particle case seems to be conceptually more complicated than the corresponding algorithm in the wave case, which may be due to the singular nature of the δ integrals in
compared to the counting problems in [23].

(2) {3} molecules: M contains one atom of deg 3.
(3) {4} molecules: M contains one atom of deg 4.

Remark 9.5. We explain the classification of elementary molecules in Definition 9.4 as follows:

(1) Note that Definition 9.4 allows for some {4} molecules and empty ends to be both good and bad; this will not cause any confusion, because in practice the property of good/non-good and bad/non-bad are always exploited independently. The rule of thumb is that, each good molecule leads to a power
gain in the estimate of the integral
in (7.6), and each bad molecule leads to a power
loss in this integral (and each normal molecule leads to no gain or loss). These gain and loss estimates easily follow from Definition 9.4 and Propositions 9.1–9.3.

(2) Note that the definition of good molecules depends on various extra restrictions imposed in Definition 9.4. In fact, these extra restrictions (corresponding to degeneracy and non-degeneracy conditions) are what motivates the splitting steps in the operation sequence. Basically, we may split into degenerate and non-degenerate sub-cases, and exploit diferent good molecules based on the extra restrictions in each diferent sub-case. We may also design diferent cutting strategies based on diferent sub-cases, which will be clear in the algorithm below (cf. the strongly and weakly degeneracies in Propositions 12.5 and 12.17, where we have a diferent cutting strategy from the main case).

Remark 9.6. Most of the elementary molecules that will occur in the algorithm (Sections 11–13) are {2}, {3}, {4} and {33A} molecules. In fact, {33B} molecules will occur only in the MAINUD algorithm (Definition 13.12), and the {44} molecule will occur only in Choice 1 in the proof of Proposition 12.5. Our construction will guarantee that the {33B} and {44} molecules are always good every time they occur.

Definition 12.1 (The algorithm UP). Define the following cutting algorithm UP. It takes as input any (regular) molecule M, which has no top fixed end at any C-atom (we henceforth abbreviate it as C-top fixed ends; same for C-bottom fixed ends).
